title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell, who wished to join the parade. Bram’s cart was damaged, its cover was loose, and the breeze was lively enough to chase a hat. Mayor Bell still wanted the biggest parade, but first the cart needed more than enthusiasm.

Ada noticed the breeze tugging ribbons in the square. “That wind is breezy,” she said, watching a scrap of paper scoot past like it had somewhere important to be. Ada told Bram about the breeze. Bram looked at the cart’s loose cover. “Then the wind may borrow the cover,” he said, “unless I tie it down first.” Ada noticed Nell peering toward the parade preparations. “I want to join,” Nell said. Ada heard her clearly and remembered the exact wish. Bram checked his cart and found the damage: one wheel wobbled, and the cart gave a sadly lopsided creak. “You are not ready,” he told it. The cart seemed to agree.

Bram tied the cart’s loose cover firmly. He tugged the knot twice. The cover stayed put, even when the breeze gave it a testing flap.

Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants to join.” Mayor Bell blinked. His parade had been designed for spectators, not a book-holding helper. “Then we shall make room,” he said.

Bram tightened the loose wheel and tested the cart with a careful push. This time it rolled straight. “Ready,” he announced. “Now you can carry something more useful than my lunch.”

Bram lent Ada the cart after securing its cover. “Now the wind can fuss all it likes,” he said. “It may flap, but it may not fly away with our cargo.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada handed the book to Nell at the square. Nell held it against her chest. “Now I can join the parade,” she said, looking delighted rather than book-buried.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell welcomed Nell into the parade with a cheerful wave. Nell joined while holding her book, and Mayor Bell cheered—not for the size of his parade, but for the newest person in it.

Nell marched happily with her book while the tied cover fluttered above the sturdy cart. Mayor Bell cheered, Ada guided the cart, and the breeze tossed ribbons around them. The parade was no longer merely big; it had become a welcoming, book-carrying whirl of smiles.

title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell, who hoped for quiet in the square. Bram’s cart was damaged, and its cover was loose; even the breeze seemed ready to make matters worse. Mayor Bell’s promised biggest parade suddenly had a very wobbly beginning.

Bram checked his cart and found the damage: one wheel wobbled, and the cart gave a sadly lopsided creak. “You are not ready,” he told it. The cart seemed to agree. Ada noticed the breeze tugging ribbons in the square. “That wind is breezy,” she said, watching a scrap of paper scoot past like it had somewhere important to be.

Bram tightened the loose wheel and tested the cart with a careful push. This time it rolled straight. “Ready,” he announced. “Now you can carry something more useful than my lunch.”

Ada noticed Nell watching the noisy preparations. “I hope Nell wants quiet,” Ada whispered. Nell nodded. That was the exact thing she wanted. Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants quiet.” Mayor Bell lowered the parade horn from his lips. “Quiet?” he said. “That is a very small sound—and perhaps a very important one.” Ada told Bram about the breeze. Bram looked at the cart’s loose cover. “Then the wind may borrow the cover,” he said, “unless I tie it down first.”

Bram tied the cart’s loose cover firmly. He tugged the knot twice. The cover stayed put, even when the breeze gave it a testing flap.

Bram lent Ada the cart after securing its cover. “Now the wind can fuss all it likes,” he said. “It may flap, but it may not fly away with our cargo.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada delivered the book to Nell beneath the tied cover. The breeze rustled above them, but the pages stayed safe. Nell accepted the book with a grateful smile.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell led a quiet book procession. No drum boomed; no horn blared. He walked proudly while Nell held her book, and the whole parade made only the soft shush of shoes.

The breeze danced around the square, lifting ribbons but not the cart’s tied cover. Under it, Nell held her book safely while Mayor Bell led a proud, quiet procession. The cart’s knots made tiny taps in the wind, like two little drumbeats keeping everyone calm.

title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell, who wanted to join Mayor Bell’s parade. Bram’s cart was ready, but its loose cover flapped in the breezy square. Ada eyed the cart, the book, and the wind. One of them clearly needed a knot.

Ada noticed the breeze tugging ribbons in the square. “That wind is breezy,” she said, watching a scrap of paper scoot past like it had somewhere important to be. Ada noticed Nell peering toward the parade preparations. “I want to join,” Nell said. Ada heard her clearly and remembered the exact wish. Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants to join.” Mayor Bell blinked. His parade had been designed for spectators, not a book-holding helper. “Then we shall make room,” he said. Ada told Bram about the breeze. Bram looked at the cart’s loose cover. “Then the wind may borrow the cover,” he said, “unless I tie it down first.”

Bram tied the cart’s loose cover firmly. He tugged the knot twice. The cover stayed put, even when the breeze gave it a testing flap.

Bram lent Ada the cart after securing its cover. “Now the wind can fuss all it likes,” he said. “It may flap, but it may not fly away with our cargo.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada handed the book to Nell at the square. Nell held it against her chest. “Now I can join the parade,” she said, looking delighted rather than book-buried.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell welcomed Nell into the parade with a cheerful wave. Nell joined while holding her book, and Mayor Bell cheered—not for the size of his parade, but for the newest person in it.

Nell marched happily with her book while the tied cover fluttered above the sturdy cart. Mayor Bell cheered, Ada guided the cart, and the breeze tossed ribbons around them. The parade was no longer merely big; it had become a welcoming, book-carrying whirl of smiles.

title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell, who was waiting in the square. The cart Bram built stood ready in his workshop, but it still belonged to him. Mayor Bell was planning the biggest parade ever—so big, he said, that even the pigeons needed tickets.

Bram rested one hand on the cart. “It is ready, and the square is still. You may borrow it, Ada—but roll gently. It is a cart, not a galloping goat.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble. Ada noticed Nell watching the noisy preparations. “I hope Nell wants quiet,” Ada whispered. Nell nodded. That was the exact thing she wanted.

Ada brought the book to Nell without a shout or a trumpet. Nell took it carefully. “Thank you,” she said, as softly as a page turning.

Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants quiet.” Mayor Bell lowered the parade horn from his lips. “Quiet?” he said. “That is a very small sound—and perhaps a very important one.” Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell led a quiet book procession. No drum boomed; no horn blared. He walked proudly while Nell held her book, and the whole parade made only the soft shush of shoes.

Nell hugged the book while the parade curled around her like a gentle ribbon. Mayor Bell’s proud smile needed no megaphone, and Ada’s cart stood ready, its loose cover resting neatly in place. Even the pigeons seemed to understand: this was a very useful kind of grand.

title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell, who hoped for quiet in the square. Bram’s cart was damaged, and its cover was loose; even the breeze seemed ready to make matters worse. Mayor Bell’s promised biggest parade suddenly had a very wobbly beginning.

Ada noticed Nell watching the noisy preparations. “I hope Nell wants quiet,” Ada whispered. Nell nodded. That was the exact thing she wanted. Ada noticed the breeze tugging ribbons in the square. “That wind is breezy,” she said, watching a scrap of paper scoot past like it had somewhere important to be. Bram checked his cart and found the damage: one wheel wobbled, and the cart gave a sadly lopsided creak. “You are not ready,” he told it. The cart seemed to agree. Ada told Bram about the breeze. Bram looked at the cart’s loose cover. “Then the wind may borrow the cover,” he said, “unless I tie it down first.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants quiet.” Mayor Bell lowered the parade horn from his lips. “Quiet?” he said. “That is a very small sound—and perhaps a very important one.”

Bram tied the cart’s loose cover firmly. He tugged the knot twice. The cover stayed put, even when the breeze gave it a testing flap.

Bram tightened the loose wheel and tested the cart with a careful push. This time it rolled straight. “Ready,” he announced. “Now you can carry something more useful than my lunch.”

Bram lent Ada the cart after securing its cover. “Now the wind can fuss all it likes,” he said. “It may flap, but it may not fly away with our cargo.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada delivered the book to Nell beneath the tied cover. The breeze rustled above them, but the pages stayed safe. Nell accepted the book with a grateful smile.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell led a quiet book procession. No drum boomed; no horn blared. He walked proudly while Nell held her book, and the whole parade made only the soft shush of shoes.

The breeze danced around the square, lifting ribbons but not the cart’s tied cover. Under it, Nell held her book safely while Mayor Bell led a proud, quiet procession. The cart’s knots made tiny taps in the wind, like two little drumbeats keeping everyone calm.

title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell in the square, but the only useful cart was damaged. Its wheel sagged like a tired knee in Bram’s workshop. Mayor Bell, meanwhile, promised the biggest parade in town, though a big promise could not carry a book.

Bram checked his cart and found the damage: one wheel wobbled, and the cart gave a sadly lopsided creak. “You are not ready,” he told it. The cart seemed to agree.

Bram tightened the loose wheel and tested the cart with a careful push. This time it rolled straight. “Ready,” he announced. “Now you can carry something more useful than my lunch.”

Ada noticed Nell watching the noisy preparations. “I hope Nell wants quiet,” Ada whispered. Nell nodded. That was the exact thing she wanted. Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants quiet.” Mayor Bell lowered the parade horn from his lips. “Quiet?” he said. “That is a very small sound—and perhaps a very important one.” Bram rested one hand on the cart. “It is ready, and the square is still. You may borrow it, Ada—but roll gently. It is a cart, not a galloping goat.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada brought the book to Nell without a shout or a trumpet. Nell took it carefully. “Thank you,” she said, as softly as a page turning.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell led a quiet book procession. No drum boomed; no horn blared. He walked proudly while Nell held her book, and the whole parade made only the soft shush of shoes.

Nell hugged the book while the parade curled around her like a gentle ribbon. Mayor Bell’s proud smile needed no megaphone, and Ada’s cart stood ready, its loose cover resting neatly in place. Even the pigeons seemed to understand: this was a very useful kind of grand.

title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell in the square, but Bram’s cart was damaged. Its wheel pointed one way while the cart pointed another—rather like a duck giving directions. Nell wanted to join Mayor Bell’s enormous parade, which had not yet made room for her.

Ada noticed Nell peering toward the parade preparations. “I want to join,” Nell said. Ada heard her clearly and remembered the exact wish. Bram checked his cart and found the damage: one wheel wobbled, and the cart gave a sadly lopsided creak. “You are not ready,” he told it. The cart seemed to agree. Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants to join.” Mayor Bell blinked. His parade had been designed for spectators, not a book-holding helper. “Then we shall make room,” he said.

Bram tightened the loose wheel and tested the cart with a careful push. This time it rolled straight. “Ready,” he announced. “Now you can carry something more useful than my lunch.”

Bram rested one hand on the cart. “It is ready, and the square is still. You may borrow it, Ada—but roll gently. It is a cart, not a galloping goat.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada handed the book to Nell at the square. Nell held it against her chest. “Now I can join the parade,” she said, looking delighted rather than book-buried.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell welcomed Nell into the parade with a cheerful wave. Nell joined while holding her book, and Mayor Bell cheered—not for the size of his parade, but for the newest person in it.

The parade rolled on with Nell at its heart, her new book held high like a bright little flag. Mayor Bell cheered, Ada grinned, and Bram’s cart carried its borrowed treasure steadily. What began as one grand parade now had one more happy marcher than anyone had planned.

title: The Parade That Carried Good News
story:
Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell, who hoped for quiet in the busy square. Bram’s cart was ready in his workshop, but the breeze was already fussing with its loose cover. Mayor Bell planned the biggest parade, complete with a horn that looked much too cheerful.

Ada noticed the breeze tugging ribbons in the square. “That wind is breezy,” she said, watching a scrap of paper scoot past like it had somewhere important to be. Ada told Bram about the breeze. Bram looked at the cart’s loose cover. “Then the wind may borrow the cover,” he said, “unless I tie it down first.”

Bram tied the cart’s loose cover firmly. He tugged the knot twice. The cover stayed put, even when the breeze gave it a testing flap.

Ada noticed Nell watching the noisy preparations. “I hope Nell wants quiet,” Ada whispered. Nell nodded. That was the exact thing she wanted. Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants quiet.” Mayor Bell lowered the parade horn from his lips. “Quiet?” he said. “That is a very small sound—and perhaps a very important one.” Bram lent Ada the cart after securing its cover. “Now the wind can fuss all it likes,” he said. “It may flap, but it may not fly away with our cargo.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada delivered the book to Nell beneath the tied cover. The breeze rustled above them, but the pages stayed safe. Nell accepted the book with a grateful smile.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell led a quiet book procession. No drum boomed; no horn blared. He walked proudly while Nell held her book, and the whole parade made only the soft shush of shoes.

The breeze danced around the square, lifting ribbons but not the cart’s tied cover. Under it, Nell held her book safely while Mayor Bell led a proud, quiet procession. The cart’s knots made tiny taps in the wind, like two little drumbeats keeping everyone calm.
